analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers into arbitration for job-related disputes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 112th Congress ended, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal arbitration law, employers can require workers to sign away their right to go to court and instead resolve disputes like wrongful firing, discrimination, or unpaid wages before a private arbitrator. This bill would make any pre-dispute agreement to arbitrate an employment dispute unenforceable, restore workers' access to federal and state courts, and narrow the current carve-out (which covers only seamen, railroad workers, and similar transportation workers) to exclude all employment contracts. Arbitration clauses negotiated between an employer and a union would still be allowed, but they could not waive a worker's right to go to court over rights protected by the Constitution or by statute.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by forced arbitration clauses, who would regain the right to take employment disputes to court instead of private arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that no pre-dispute arbitration agreement requiring arbitration of an employment dispute is valid or enforceable [S3].
It defines an employment dispute as any dispute between employer and employee arising from the employment relationship [S2].

It broadens the existing exemption, which covers only seamen, railroad employees, and similar interstate transportation workers, so that all employment contracts fall outside federal arbitration law [S2].
Even where a union contract contains arbitration, employees keep the right to go to court to enforce constitutional and statutory rights [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would lose the ability to route employee claims into private arbitration, and the arbitration industry, which would lose employment-dispute business.

drawbacks.text: Employers argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for resolving disputes, and the bill would remove that option in the employment context [S2].
The bill would still allow employer-union arbitration provisions, so its protections depend on whether a worker is covered by a collective bargaining agreement or an individual contract [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real: workers under forced arbitration clauses would regain court access for disputes like discrimination, wage claims, and wrongful termination, where arbitration often limits remedies and discovery. The main cost falls on employers, who lose a cheaper dispute-resolution channel, though the bill leaves union-negotiated arbitration intact and preserves the speed benefits of voluntarily agreed arbitration after a dispute arises.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill on March 8, 2012 [S1].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
A week later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law [S5].
No further action appears in the record, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 without the bill advancing [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who rely on forced arbitration clauses keep the current system, and arbitration providers keep the employment-dispute business.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban enforcement of pre-dispute employment arbitration agreements.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it sat at subcommittee referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or recorded positions beyond the sponsor; the bill drew no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of any potential support or opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Arbitration and alternative dispute resolution providers
industries.note: Employment arbitration is a fee-generating line of business for private arbitration firms; banning mandatory pre-dispute employment arbitration would remove much of that market. Workers' ability to reach a public court is exactly what these providers' contracts take away.

Employers would lose the ability to require workers to sign away court access as a condition of employment, meaning employee claims over firing, discrimination, and wages could be heard in court with public procedures and appeals.
